summaries.summary: Keywords are computational sociolinguistics, dehumanization, lexical variation, language change, media, New York Times, and LGBTQ.
The paper warns that it contains material that some may find offensive or upsetting.
Despite increasing acceptance and legal successes, LGBTQ people face hate and violence, with dehumanization expressed through subtle linguistic manipulations in mainstream media.
No known large-scale analyses of dehumanization and media representation exist, though such analysis is crucial for studying long-term change and broader media discourse.
Linguistics and computer science offer methods for large-scale dehumanization study that can reveal linguistic variations and changes missed by qualitative analysis.
The authors develop a computational linguistic framework for lexical dehumanization signals and apply it to LGBTQ representations in the New York Times over three decades.

The paper bridges computational modeling, sociolinguistics, and dehumanization research, with implications for bias detection, hate speech detection, abusive language detection, and language variation.
Section SECREF4 introduces computational linguistic methods to quantify several components of dehumanization.
This first known computational work on dehumanization draws on subjective language detection, lexicon-based resources, syntactic form, and biased language classification.
Related methods analyze implicit social biases, racial bias, historical bias, power, agency, gender bias, condescension, microagressions, othering language, hate speech, and abusive language.
Gender and racial bias appear in NLP systems across toxicity detection, sentiment analysis, coreference resolution, language identification, and other areas, prompting mitigation work.

Related computational research investigates media discourse on sociopolitical issues through framing detection, supervised classification, unsupervised methods, lexical cues, political slant, and polarization.
Paragraphs were optimal for analysis, so paragraph-level scores average NRC VAD lexicon valence scores over all matching words or lemmas.
The authors extract subject-verb-object tuples with target group labels using the Spacy dependency parser and average connotation frame perspective scores.
Connotation Frames are more precise than word-counting valence analysis but exclude much target-group data by limiting analysis to SVO triples.
Word embedding neighbor valence can reveal negative evaluations, diachronic connotation changes, and meaning variation between related group labels.
Vermin metaphors are prominent in dehumanization and may appear indirectly through associated verbs, which metaphor detection systems cannot easily quantify.
Table TABREF18 overviews the four studied elements of dehumanization and the lexical techniques used to quantify them.
The case study captures the New York Times institution's attitudes toward LGBTQ people using news articles, quotes, paraphrases, opinion articles, and all relevant paragraph text.
Qualitative analysis of word embedding neighbors reveals variation and change in LGBTQ group label social meanings related to dehumanizing language.
Qualitative evaluation of several hundred highest and lowest average valence paragraphs suggests high scores express positive evaluations and low scores negative evaluations.
Paragraph-level valence analysis has shortcomings involving short subtitles, skewed positive words, kinship terms, and mischaracterized examples in Table TABREF30.
Paragraph-level valence often aligns with evaluations but is affected by topic words, perspective disentanglement, and repeated negative contexts around LGBTQ identity labels.
Connotation frames identify negative perspectives toward LGBTQ labels through verbs like committed and positive perspectives through praise, as shown in Table TABREF36.
Table TABREF37 shows mislabeled connotation frame cases involving contradiction, negation, sarcasm, Al Qaeda, and stereotypes about gay people.
Connotation frames use less context than the NRC VAD lexicon labeled for 20,000 words but make finer attitude distinctions and retain quotes and paraphrases.
Although no New York Times writers directly compare LGBTQ people to vermin, subtle invocations and explicit arguments against the metaphor appear in Table TABREF62.
The framework studied LGBTQ dehumanization in the New York Times from 1986 to 2015 and found increasingly humanizing descriptions over 30 years.
Limitations include measurements affected by topics and events, difficulty disambiguating perspectives, and use of word2vec despite potential contextualized embedding methods.
Lack of ground truth labels prevented supervised methods and quantitative evaluations, though best-worst scaling could enable unified dehumanization measurement.
The focus on lexical cues omits definite plurals, part of speech, non-lexical signals, and discourse-level analysis such as direct quotes.
The New York Times case study is limited by one data source, Standard American English, aggregated LGBTQ representation, and focus on gay and homosexual.
The authors hope to improve media representation and online safety while acknowledging ethical implications and potential issues of their work.
The quantification methods are biased and potentially harmful, including anti-LGBTQ lexicon biases and biased New York Times word2vec training data.
Using computational methods to represent people as sequences of numbers is inherently dehumanizing despite hopes to humanize and empower marginalized groups.
This first known computational linguistic study of dehumanization contributes frameworks for linguistic variation, large-scale analysis, media bias, and abusive language online.
The authors thank Rob Voigt, Chris Potts, Penny Eckert, David Jurgens, Ceren Budak, Anna-Marie Sprenger, Ismael Mendoza, and the NWAV-46 audience.
The lexical semantic analysis quantifies linguistic correlates of psychological dehumanization processes, including likening target groups to non-human entities and especially vermin metaphors.
Disgust, moral exclusion, essentialist beliefs, and exaggerated intergroup differences are described as important elements contributing to dehumanizing perceptions of target groups.
Prior research describes extremely negative evaluations, delegitimization, moral exclusion, psychological distancing, objectification, and denial of subjectivity as dehumanization-related processes.
Denial of agency is a dehumanization component involving denial of affective mental states, behavioral potential, or cognitive mental states.
The authors introduce and quantify lexical correlates for negative evaluations of a target group, denial of agency, moral disgust, and non-human metaphors, particularly vermin.
Extremely negative evaluations are hypothesized to appear in low-valence words and phrases, measured through paragraph-level valence analysis, Connotation Frames, and word embedding neighbor valence.
Paragraph-level valence analysis measures average valence over words using the NRC VAD lexicon, with scores from zero to one for 20,000 English words.
Paragraph-level valence analysis can be too coarse because nearby negative text may not reflect sentiment directed toward the target group.
BIBREF22's Connotation Frames Lexicon annotates 900 English verbs with writer perspective scores ranging from -0.87 to 0.8 toward subjects and objects.
The authors extract subject-verb-object tuples containing target group labels with the Spacy dependency parser and average Connotation Frames perspective scores.
Connotation Frames are more precise than word-counting valence analysis but exclude much data by limiting analysis to SVO triples.
Word embedding neighbor valence uses proximity of social group label vectors to negative words to study negative evaluations, diachronic connotation changes, and meaning variation.

A regression-based sentiment prediction adaptation directly induced valence scores from group label vectors, yielding similar results to nearest neighbor valence but difficult qualitative interpretation.
Denial of agency concerns lack of attributed control over actions or decisions, and existing lexicons provide resources for measuring its lexical signals.

BIBREF25's extension of Connotation Frames for agency distinguishes high-agency active decision-makers from low-agency passive entities through verbs such as searched, waited, attack, praise, doubts, needs, and owes.
The agency lexicon covers nearly 2000 transitive and intransitive verbs, and the authors calculate the fraction of subject-verb pairs with high agency for group-label subjects.
The NRC VAD lexicon's dominance scores between zero and one for 20,000 English words provide a power-related proxy for denial of agency using average dominance of the 1000 nearest neighbors.
The authors also induced dominance scores directly from group label vector representations by adapting regression-based sentiment prediction from BIBREF62.
Moral disgust is operationalized using Moral Foundations theory and BIBREF64 lexicons, with the Moral Disgust dictionary containing over thirty words and stems.
A frequency-weighted Moral Disgust concept vector is built from word embeddings, and cosine similarity with group label vectors measures implicit associations with moral disgust.
A frequency-weighted Vermin concept vector is built from specified vermin words, and cosine similarity with social group labels quantifies metaphorical associations with vermin.

Qualitative evaluation of several hundred highest and lowest average valence paragraphs suggests high scores express positive evaluations of LGBTQ individuals and low scores express negative evaluations.
Qualitative investigation finds binary agency labels reasonably accurate, with develop and endorse attributing high agency and face and acknowledge attributing low agency to LGBTQ subjects.
The lexical-level framework uses the NRC VAD lexicon, Connotation Frames lexicons, and the Moral Foundations Dictionary, highlighting tradeoffs between accuracy and interpretability.
Future work could include psychological distancing, essentialism, denial of subjectivity, and distinctions between animalistic and mechanistic dehumanization.
Ridge regression models trained on 85% of NRC VAD lexicon words and tested on 15% directly predict group label valence from yearly Word2Vec embeddings.
Additional yearly ridge regression models with word embedding features directly induce dominance scores from target group label representations using NRC VAD dominance lexicon scores.
American acceptance of LGBTQ people and rights increased, with legal approval rising from 43% in 1977 to 73% in 2019 and same-sex marriage support from 35% to 61%.
The study compares gay and homosexual, describing Gallup wording changes, GLAAD's objections, clinical and sexual connotations, and New York Times usage restrictions.
Label choice affects attitudes, as “homosexual rights” reduced support in 2012, especially among high authoritarians, motivating expectations of more dehumanizing contexts for homosexual.
The case study uses New York Times articles from January 1986 to December 2015 across sections, with distributional methods using all data and other techniques using LGBTQ-term paragraphs.
Acronym labels were matched insensitively, queer and trans were excluded, and non-news sections such as “Arts”, “Theater”, and “Movies” were filtered out.
The LGBTQ corpus contains 93,977 paragraphs and 7.36 million tokens, with 1986 least represented and 2012 most represented.
American and Americans are included as comparison labels to test whether LGBTQ changes reflect broader language change, though American(s) is not a neutral control.
Figure FIGREF20 shows homosexual decreasing over time, gay, lesbian, and bisexual increasing later, and lgbt and transgender emerging after 2000.
Table TABREF22 shows 1986 LGBTQ associations with sexual deviancy, 2000 associations with civil rights, and 2015 associations with identity, with abortion nearby all three years.
Table TABREF23 shows gay and homosexual differing from 1986, with gay linked to discrimination and activism and homosexual linked to sexual activity.
Homosexual's pejoration continued from 1986 through 2000 and 2015, while gay became associated with marriage equality and identity.
Figure FIGREF27 uses the NRC VAD Valence Lexicon, whose LGBTQ terms have low valence scores, and removes them to isolate New York Times linguistic signals.
Figure FIGREF27 shows gay and all LGBTQ terms in significantly more positive paragraphs than homosexual, while American is more negative and valence increases over time.
Paragraph-level valence suggests LGBTQ groups became more positively evaluated, but homosexual between 2001 and 2015 did not improve like other labels.
The measurement rejects the hypothesis that LGBTQ groups were more negatively evaluated than American(s), while showing substantial language change and label-context variation.

Table TABREF29 shows high-valence paragraphs emphasize equal rights and advocacy, while low-valence paragraphs concern violence, disease, international issues, dehumanizing quotes, and negative portrayals.
Table TABREF30 shows shortcomings from short subtitles, misleading positive words, and highly positive kinship terms in the NRC VAD Valence Lexicon.
Figure FIGREF34 shows writer perspective using the Connotation Frames lexicon, with wide variation from sparsity and only 39 triples for homosexual in 2015.
Homosexual receives significantly more negative perspective than gay, while perspectives toward any LGBTQ term, gay, and American increase over time and homosexual decreases.
Connotation frames show LGBTQ groups more positively evaluated over time, while homosexual undergoes pejoration and increasingly expresses negative attitudes.
Figure FIGREF40 shows American's 1000 nearest neighbors have significantly greater valence than LGBTQ representations, while all LGBTQ neighbors remain below 0.5 but increase over time.
Figure FIGREF40 shows homosexual's neighbors have significantly lower valence than gay's and become more negative over time, while gay's increase is nonsignificant.
Table TABREF42 links 1999 low-valence associations to Matthew Shepard's October 1998 murder and media emphasis on gruesome details.
In 2014, gay and all LGBTQ terms were associated with harassing, intimidation, stigma, anti-LGBTQ laws and attitudes in Uganda and Russia, and the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi.
In 1993, homosexual's nearby words had the highest average valence, with unique neighbors connected to controversy over LGBTQ people serving in the military.
Figure FIGREF45 shows agency from Connotation Frames, with large yearly variance from data sparsity, especially for homosexual, and five-year intervals for visualization.
Gay occurs with significantly higher agency than homosexual, all four labels decrease in agency over 30 years, and homosexual decreases most sharply.
Figure FIGREF45 suggests LGBTQ groups face greater denial of agency than American, homosexual more than gay, and denial of agency increased over time.
Table TABREF47 shows reasonably accurate binary agency labels, with develop and endorse indicating high agency and face and acknowledge indicating low agency.
Low-agency labels seemed accurate, but some high-agency labels were mischaracterized, including homosexual modifying relationships rather than people in a religious debate.
A 1996 paragraph describes a stark division in Judaism and Orthodox rabbinical groups' belief that homosexual relationships violate Jewish law.
Figure FIGREF55 shows American least associated with Moral Disgust, homosexual closer than gay, and weakening associations for all LGBTQ terms and gay over time.
All LGBTQ labels are more associated with Moral Disgust than American, but associations weaken over time, while homosexual remains more associated than gay and increases recently.
Table TABREF23 and Table TABREF57 support moral disgust as a mechanism, with rapid late 1980s and early 1990s changes likely due to decreasing AIDS attention.
Figure FIGREF60 shows American furthest from Vermin, homosexual closer than gay, and all LGBTQ terms and gay becoming less associated over time.
LGBTQ groups are more implicitly associated with vermin than American, but this weakens over time, while homosexual's association does not significantly change.
Although no New York Times writers directly compare LGBTQ people to vermin, Table TABREF62 shows subtle invocations and explicit arguments against the metaphor.
Gay and homosexual differ across four dehumanization components, with homosexual more negative, lower agency, closer to moral disgust and vermin, and increasingly dehumanizing after about 2000.
Ethical implications include excluding queer and trans, minimizing diversity through aggregation, and emphasizing gay and homosexual at the expense of other marginalized labels.
Word embeddings capture semantic relations and change, contain real-world biases, and can identify stereotypes about social groups and their changes over time.
The authors preprocess data, train 100-dimensional word2vec skip-gram embeddings with specified parameters, use cosine similarity, initialize yearly models, and zero-center and normalize embeddings.
Group label vectors are frequency-weighted centroids of morphological forms, and valence is the average NRC VAD valence lexicon valence of 1000 nearest neighbors.
Using all New York Times data, yearly vector space models were created, and Table TABREF22 shows ten nearest neighbors to all LGBTQ terms with filters applied.
Figure FIGREF40 shows 1000-neighbor valence for gay, homosexual, all LGBTQ terms, and American, with American significantly more positive and all LGBTQ terms increasing over time.
Because word embeddings are hard to interpret from small samples, the authors assess LGBTQ terms' unique nearest neighbors in several outlier years.
The most negative year for gay and all LGBTQ terms since 1999 was 2014, with unique neighbors and themes involving Uganda, Russia, and the 2014 Winter Olympics in Sochi.
Figure FIGREF45 shows group label agency from Connotation Frames, with large yearly variance from data sparsity and average agency shown over five-year intervals.
Figure FIGREF51 shows 1000-neighbor dominance from the NRC VAD Dominance Lexicon, with American highest, gay above homosexual, and differing temporal trends.
NRC VAD Dominance Lexicon dominance helps operationalize denial of agency, suggesting LGBTQ groups experience greater denial than American and differing temporal dynamics from Connotation Frames.
VAD Dominance Lexicon averages correspond to denial of agency, with high-agency words near gay and low-agency words near homosexual in 2015 and 1986.
Outlier-year analysis links homosexual's high 1993 dominance to “Don't Ask, Don't Tell” military discourse and gay's low 1999 dominance to Matthew Shepard's death.
The authors train yearly ridge regression models on zero-centered, normalized Word2Vec embeddings to predict valence from NRC VAD lexicon scores using 85% training and 15% test data.
Figure FIGREF67 shows directly-induced valence trends, with American most positive, homosexual most negative, and homosexual's predicted valence decreasing from 2001 to 2015.
Figure FIGREF69 shows predicted dominance from ridge regression, with American significantly greater than LGBTQ terms and no significant difference between gay and homosexual.
The authors suggest regression features could not capture subtle dominance distinctions because average neighbor dominance differences were small and word2vec predicted just over a third of variance.
